content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, authors propose to address the key issue in the phrase detection task namely how to sample the negatives to obtain the discriminative models. A CFCDNet is proposed to differentiate between phrases through both noun and adjective views. The performance gains have been observed on the benchmark datasets to validate the effectiveness of proposed sampling strategies.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
Authors consider from both noun and adjective point of view to sample the hard negatives to increase the discriminative ability of the detectors, i.e., the semantically close concepts are grouped together, and model is required to differentiate between a region of interest and its unrelated concepts, as for the adjectives, the model is forced to select from one of the mutually excluded phrases.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The proposed approach is well is clearly explained in the paper. The writing is fluent and easy to understand. However, the novelty of the paper needs to be carefully leveraged.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The motivation is quite clear and easy to follow, however, certain concerns raise against the experimental comparisons:

1) the ablation studies seem to be lacked to analyze the importance of two proposed sample selection strategies.

2) hard negative mining is applied in the proposed model, what about applying the same mining strategy to the sota models?

3) seems such sample selection can be inserted to the training of sota models, did authors evaluate the performance of such combination?

content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength 
The performance compared with current algorithms seems quite convincing.

Weaknesses
1. The paper is quite poorly written and I am quite confused with the proposed methods. It is unclear whether CFCD-Net and FGM are two separate modules or CFCD-Net contains NCC and FGM. It seems it is the latter. However, as suggested in the contribution, CFCD-Net improves 1.5-2 average mAP but FGM improves 1-4 average mAP, which is contradictory. 
2. The authors claim that hard negative mining may miss a large distribution of negatives. And NCC is proposed to address this limitation. However, the authors also use hard negative mining in this work. Why? It seems it is also contradictory and confusing.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work focuses on the task of phrase detection, which, compares with existing textual ground/referring expression task is more challenging as it requires to detect if the phrase exist or not. Such tasks requires the model to be capable to discern the trivial differences of textual queries and grasp the semantic on both coarse&fine levels. The proposed method circles around this intuition and models the contrastive training on both aspects and observe obvious performance improvements.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

1. Clear motivation and method. 
2. Good empirical results on the benchmark. 

Weaknesses:
1. Introduction part can be improved if there's more contents dsecribes the motivation in the begining. Current introduction may confuse the readers as too it dives into details hastily. 
2. I have some doubts about the phrase grounding task with existing efforts. See detailed comments.
3. Concern about authorship anonymity.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The motivation of the work is novel, and the provides with the source codes.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper focuses on the phrase grounding task and aims to resolve the coarse/fine semantic alignent challenge which brings substantial performance improvement on phrase grounding task. The proposed contrastive learning schema makes sense and presented empirical results validate the claimed improvement. In overall I think this is a good submission which further advances the prior phrase grounding efforts with the new contrastive schema, and the proposed coarse/fine learning schema seems effective as experiments suggest. 

I have some doubts and concerns:

1. About introduction writing: as a reader that did not closely follow the recent ongoings of phrase grounding, it confuses me regards the differences of phrase grounding and referring expression/textual grounding task. The introduction presents a very comprehensive picture of the main focus, key challenge of this task, yet contains too much details and related works. I suggest the author to re-organize the introduction part and put more contents explaining the motivation, impact, and differences with previous tasks of phrase grounding before getting to the details. 

2. "Phrase grounding task aims to identify image regions related to free form phrases": following my previous comment, what differetiates phrase grounding with textual grounding task? Is the only difference is determine the existent of free form phrases? In such a case what makes such case differerence with previous work [1] where the model encounters non-existing counterfactual queries?

3. Concern regards the authorship anonymity. It comes to my notice that the author's name appeared in provided source codes, which violates the anonymous polic of ICLR. I understand this is not likely to be disclosed purposefully and rejecting a good subimssion for this reason is not reasonable. So I urge the authors to properly address this during rebuttal period.

[1] "Modularized textual grounding for counterfactual resilience." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2019.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a coarse-to-fine-grained approach for phrase detection. It uses a phrase detector to group phrases and a fine-grained module to force the model into selecting only one applicable phrase.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The paper structure is well-organized and easy to follow.

Weakness:
1. Assume that some phrases are similar in concept to some extent (eg: red apple and red cup, because they have similar colors), but are labeled in different concept groups in the proposed method. This will result in the corruption of "phrase-image region" pairs which have similar semantics, resulting in performance degradation. The authors should supplement experiments to explain that the concept set proposed in this paper is not an overfitting setting.

2. Due to the lack of an intuitive figure for the proposed method, it is difficult to get the specific practices and intentions of the authors.

3. The logic of the Related Work is confusing. The authors should first summarize and explain the shortcomings of the existing methods and then introduce the proposed method.

4. As far as I know, GLIP, R-CLIP, MDETR are not specially designed for phrase location. The authors should address the fairness of this comparison and supplement more recent work for comparison. 

5. The comparison in Table 3 is unfair. In the case of different training sets, the comparison of model training time is meaningless.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The structure of this paper is complete, but the details of the proposed method are not clear enough, and the rationality needs further explanation.

content.title: From Coarse to Fine-grained Concept based Discrimination for Phrase Detection
content.abstract: Phrase detection requires methods to identify if a phrase is relevant to an image and localize it if applicable. A key challenge in training more discriminative phrase detection models is sampling negatives. However, sampling techniques from prior work focus primarily on hard, often noisy, negatives disregarding the broader distribution of negative samples. To address this problem, we introduce CFCD-Net, a phrase detector that differentiates between phrases through two novels methods. First, we generate groups that consist of semantically similar words we call  concepts (\eg \{dog, cat, horse, ...\} vs.\ \{car, truck, ...\}), and then train our CFCD-Net to discriminate between a region of interest and its unrelated concepts. Second, for phrases containing fine-grained mutually-exclusive words (\eg colors), we force the model into selecting only one applicable phrase for each region using our novel fine grained module (FGM). We evaluate our approach on the Flickr30K Entities and RefCOCO+ datasets, where we improve mAP over the state-of-the-art by 1.5-2 points. When considering only the phrases affected by our fine-grained reasoning module, we improve by 3-4 points on both datasets
